name: Design a Maps and Routing Service
intent: Serve map tiles to hundreds of millions of people and find a fast route across a continent in milliseconds, with an ETA that follows live traffic and a route that changes when the road ahead jams.
codeTitle: Dijkstra and A* on a road grid
finalIntro: One driver asking for a route, driving it, and being sent around a jam.
prompt: Design a maps service. The app shows a map that the user can pan and zoom, finds the fastest driving route between two points anywhere on a continent with about 25 million intersections, shows an ETA that reflects live traffic, and changes the route while the user drives if the road ahead slows down.
functional: Show a map at any zoom level and let the user pan and zoom smoothly
Find the fastest route between two points, with alternatives
Show an ETA that accounts for current and expected traffic
Collect live traffic from the phones of drivers and apply it to the roads
Reroute a driver who is navigating when the road ahead slows down
Apply map updates such as new roads, closures and changed turn rules
nonFunctional: Map tiles load in under 100 ms at the 95th percentile, from a nearby cache
A route query across the continent answers in under 100 ms, and a typical one in a few milliseconds
Traffic on a road is visible in routes and ETAs within about a minute
Handle about 450,000 tile requests per second and 13,000 route queries per second at the peak
Stay available when a region of the map servers or the traffic feed fails
The ETA is usually within 10% of the real travel time
A bad map update can be rolled back quickly

firstAttempt.text: One server holds the road graph in memory and runs Dijkstra's algorithm for every request. Map images are drawn on demand from the map database for each request, and traffic is not used: every road has a fixed speed.
limits: Dijkstra settles every intersection closer than the destination, so a 60 km trip touches about 450,000 intersections and takes more than 100 ms on one core
Drawing each tile on demand makes the renderer the bottleneck, and zoomed-out tiles cover enormous amounts of data
With fixed speeds the ETA ignores rush hour, accidents and closures, so it is often far off
One machine is one point of failure, and one process cannot answer 13,000 searches a second
A map update means restarting the server and loading the whole graph again

quiz.question: A* and Dijkstra return the same cheapest route on a road grid, but A* settles fewer intersections. Why is the answer still exact?
options: The estimate never overestimates the remaining cost, so A* never skips a cheaper route
A* only looks at fast roads, which are always the cheapest
A* remembers the answers of earlier queries
The estimate is rounded up, which makes the search safer
quiz.explanation: A* orders the search by the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to go. If the estimate is a lower bound, such as straight-line distance at the top speed, the first time it reaches the destination the route is optimal. Traffic only slows roads, so the bound stays valid when live traffic is applied.

quiz.question: A contraction hierarchy answers a continental query in about a thousand settled nodes, but a new traffic snapshot arrives every minute. What is the main problem and the usual fix?
options: The query becomes inexact, so switch to Dijkstra
The shortcuts depend on the edge weights, so a new snapshot needs a rebuild, and the fix is a customizable hierarchy that keeps the node order and only recomputes the shortcut weights
The hierarchy needs more memory than the graph, so use a larger machine
Traffic can only be applied to the tiles, not to the graph
quiz.explanation: Shortcuts store the cost of the path they replace, so they are only right for the weights they were built from. A customizable hierarchy fixes the expensive part, the node order, from the road structure, and recomputes only the shortcut weights when traffic changes, which takes seconds instead of minutes.

quiz.question: An accident closes a motorway and 40,000 navigating drivers are told to leave it by the same side road at the same time. What is the real risk?
options: The side road is overloaded and becomes slower than the motorway was
The ETA service crashes because of the number of updates
The tile cache fills up with outdated tiles
The phones run out of battery
quiz.explanation: Each driver's route is cheapest given the traffic data, but the data does not yet include the drivers who are about to arrive. Giving everyone the same answer creates a new jam. Routers spread drivers over alternatives, add penalty to roads that many routes use, and reroute only when the gain is clearly worth it.

steps.title: Serve the map as a tile pyramid from a CDN
steps.problem: Drawing a fresh image for each request is slow, and a map of the world at street level is far too large to send in one piece.
steps.fix: Cut the world into square tiles in a pyramid. Zoom level 0 is one tile for the world, and each level has four times as many tiles as the one above, so level 14 has about 268 million. A tile is addressed by zoom, x and y, so its URL never changes and it can be cached by anything. Tiles are rendered ahead of time in batch down to a chosen level, stored as vector data that the phone draws or as images, and served through a CDN so that most requests never reach the origin. Deeper levels are rendered on demand and then cached.
steps.tradeoff: Reads become cheap and cacheable, and the origin sees only about 5% of the 450,000 requests per second. The cost is storage that grows by four times with every level, about 700 GB for 360 million tiles that have content down to level 14 and about 3.6 TB with one more level, and stale tiles after a map update, which have to be replaced or versioned.

steps.title: Partition the road graph into regions behind a route service
steps.problem: One process cannot hold and search every road, and a single machine cannot answer 13,000 route queries a second.
steps.fix: Model the roads as a graph: intersections are nodes, road segments are directed edges with a travel time, and turn restrictions are part of the model. Cut the continent into regions of about a million intersections along natural boundaries such as rivers and sparse areas, so that few roads cross a boundary. Each region lives on its own group of replicas. The nodes on a boundary form a small overlay graph that links the regions together, so a long query searches the start region, the overlay and the end region, and does not touch the regions in between. A gateway sends each query to the route service that owns its start.
steps.tradeoff: Memory and traffic updates are split into pieces and each region can be scaled and replaced on its own. The price is that a good route sometimes crosses a boundary, so the overlay has to be kept correct, and the query that spans several regions is slower and harder to cache than one that stays inside.

steps.title: Preprocess the graph so a query settles about a thousand nodes
steps.problem: Even inside a region, Dijkstra settles every intersection closer than the destination: about 450,000 for a 60 km trip, which is around 110 ms on one core and 1,500 cores at the peak.
steps.fix: Spend effort before the query. A* steers the search toward the destination with a lower bound on the remaining time, such as straight-line distance at the top speed, which keeps the answer exact and usually settles a third as many nodes. A contraction hierarchy goes much further: it ranks intersections by importance, contracts the least important first, and adds a shortcut edge whenever removing a node would make a path longer. A query searches only upward in rank from both ends and meets at a top-ranked node, settling around a thousand nodes. A builder produces the hierarchy for each region offline.
steps.tradeoff: A query costs well under a millisecond, and the cores needed at the peak fall from about 1,500 to about 10. The hierarchy has to be rebuilt when weights change, and it needs about 2.5 times the memory. Fixed preprocessing therefore suits stable roads, and traffic needs the next step to be handled cheaply.

steps.title: Turn phone positions into live edge weights
steps.problem: Fixed speeds ignore rush hour, accidents and closures, and every route and ETA built on them is wrong exactly when drivers care most.
steps.fix: Navigating phones report their position every few seconds, about 100,000 reports a second for 500,000 drivers, into a queue. A stream job snaps each report to a road segment (map matching), computes the speed of each segment over a one-minute window, and discards outliers and segments with too few reports, using the historical speed for that time of week instead. The result is a table of current weights for every edge, which the route service reads. A* and a customizable hierarchy accept new weights without changing their structure: the hierarchy keeps its node order and recomputes only the shortcut weights, which takes seconds rather than a full rebuild.
steps.tradeoff: Routes and ETAs follow what is happening on the road, within about a minute. The cost is a stream pipeline to run, weights that are noisy where few drivers are, and a privacy duty: reports must be anonymous and kept only as long as needed to compute a speed.

steps.title: Compute the ETA and reroute drivers on the move
steps.problem: A road that is clear now may be jammed in twenty minutes when the driver gets there, and a driver who is already on the way needs to hear about a jam ahead, not behind.
steps.fix: The ETA service prices each segment of the route with the traffic expected at the moment the driver will reach it: current speed near the start, blending into the typical speed for that time of week further away. Every navigating session is checked again at each traffic refresh, only for the part of the route that is still ahead. If an alternative saves more than a threshold, such as two minutes or 10%, the push service tells the phone to switch. To stop a herd from taking the same side road, alternatives share the extra load and the threshold keeps small gains from causing flips.
steps.tradeoff: ETAs are much closer to reality and drivers avoid jams that formed after they left. Checking 500,000 sessions every minute adds about 8,300 queries a second and a push channel, and too eager a router makes the ETA jump around and sends everybody to the same detour.

steps.title: Publish map updates safely and degrade gracefully
steps.problem: Roads open and close every day, and a bad update, such as a reversed one-way street, can send every car down the wrong road.
steps.fix: A map data pipeline merges new sources, validates them (the graph stays connected, no road has an impossible speed, sample routes still work) and produces a versioned snapshot of the graph and the changed tiles. The hierarchy for each region is built from the snapshot, and routers load the new version next to the old one and switch over by region, starting with a small canary. Only the tiles in the changed area are re-rendered and given new version names, so they do not need purging. If the traffic feed is late, the router falls back to historical speeds, and if a region fails, a replica or a neighbouring zone takes over.
steps.tradeoff: A bad update is caught early and reverted with a switch, and the service keeps working with older or less precise data. The price is two versions in memory during a switch, a pipeline with real validation to build, and slower freshness for rare map edits.

failures.scenario: The traffic feed stops or runs late
failures.impact: Weights get old, so routes and ETAs lag behind jams that already exist, and a stuck feed could freeze wrong speeds forever.
failures.answer: Every weight carries a timestamp. Weights older than a few minutes are blended back toward the historical speed for that time of week and are dropped when they are very old. The ETA display marks that traffic is not live, and an alert fires on the age of the newest window.

failures.scenario: A map update reverses a one-way street
failures.impact: Routes send drivers against traffic or avoid a good road, and the error reaches every user as soon as the new graph is loaded.
failures.answer: Validation compares routes between a fixed set of origin and destination pairs on the old and new snapshots, and blocks a release that changes too many of them. The rollout is by region with a canary first, watches the rate of reroutes and complaints, and a switch returns the routers to the previous version in seconds.

failures.scenario: A replica that owns a region of the graph crashes in the middle of a query
failures.impact: Queries starting in that region fail or time out, and rush-hour load lands on the surviving replicas.
failures.answer: Health checks remove the crashed replica and the gateway retries on another one with a short deadline. A second request can be sent after a short delay for slow replicas. Each region has several replicas that load the same snapshot, so a replacement only needs to load its region, not the continent.

failures.scenario: An accident sends 40,000 drivers to the same side road
failures.impact: The detour jams within minutes, ETAs jump, and drivers get new reroutes back to the original road.
failures.answer: The router adds a penalty to roads that many active routes already use, offers alternatives instead of one best route, and only reroutes when the saving is larger than a threshold. Reroutes are spread over a short time window, and the traffic model includes the expected load of the drivers it has just sent.

failures.scenario: A map update invalidates millions of tiles at once and every phone asks for them
failures.impact: The CDN misses together, the origin and renderer are flooded, and maps load slowly or not at all.
failures.answer: New tiles get a new version in their URL and are pushed to the CDN before the app is told the version exists. Only tiles inside the changed area are renewed, and the CDN merges identical requests for one tile so that the origin renders it once.

alternatives.title: What a tile contains

options.name: Raster images (PNG or JPEG)
options.pro: Simple for any client, and the look is fixed on the server
options.con: Large, blurry between zoom levels and a new style needs every tile redrawn

options.name: Vector tiles drawn on the phone
options.pro: Small, sharp at any zoom, restyleable and rotatable on the client
options.con: The phone needs a renderer, and drawing costs battery

alternatives.pick: Vector tiles for the base map, with raster only for old or weak clients and for satellite images.

alternatives.title: How to speed up the shortest path

options.name: Dijkstra with regions
options.pro: Simplest, always exact, and weights can change at any moment
options.con: Hundreds of thousands of settled nodes per query across a region

options.name: A* with a straight-line bound
options.pro: No preprocessing and still exact, usually about three times fewer nodes
options.con: The bound is weak on roads with very different speeds, so it does not reach the speed of a hierarchy

options.name: Contraction hierarchy
options.pro: About a thousand nodes per query on a whole continent
options.con: Needs preprocessing, and a plain hierarchy has to be rebuilt when weights change

options.name: Customizable hierarchy
options.pro: Keeps the node order and recomputes only the weights, so live traffic costs seconds
options.con: Somewhat slower queries than a plain hierarchy and a more complex implementation

alternatives.pick: A customizable hierarchy for the main road network, with A* as a fallback for rare cases like avoid-tolls profiles.

alternatives.title: How to cut the graph into regions

options.name: Fixed geographic grid cells
options.pro: Trivial to compute and easy to find the region that owns a point
options.con: Cuts cities in two, so many roads cross the boundaries

options.name: Partition by minimum cut of the road network
options.pro: Few boundary nodes, so the overlay is small and queries are fast
options.con: Needs a partitioning tool and the regions are irregular

alternatives.pick: Minimum-cut regions of similar size, found offline, with a lookup grid on top to find the region of a point.

alternatives.title: How often to refresh traffic

options.name: Every few seconds
options.pro: Very fresh, especially after an accident
options.con: Noisy weights and a heavy pipeline for little real change

options.name: About once a minute
options.pro: Smooth enough to trust, and the weights can be applied in seconds
options.con: A jam can exist for up to a minute before it shows up

options.name: Every 15 minutes
options.con: ETAs and reroutes lag behind, so drivers meet the jam first

alternatives.pick: About one minute, with faster updates only for closures that a human or a sensor reports.
